Stage 4 · Grammar

Four ways of talking about later

English has no future tense. It has forms you choose between, and the choice says how settled the thing is.

1 · Look at these lines from the two recordings.
From the listening
  • a  There will probably be more jobs in the health care sector.
  • b  We are going to have self-driving vehicles.
  • c  I’m taking a course in app design at the University of Westminster.
  • d  It starts next week.
  • e  It is going to be quite hard to get a good job straightaway.
  • f  I might find a job there too.
2 · Answer the three questions about the lines above.
1Both a and e are predictions. What makes the speaker choose going to in e?
2What is the difference between c and d?

3 · Read the table.
FormWhat it doesExample from the programme
will / won’ta prediction or opinion about later, often with think, probably, I expectThere will probably be more jobs in health care.
willa decision taken at the moment of speakingI think I’ll be an auto transport analyst!
be going toan intention decided before nowI’m going to work in my parents’ shop.
be going toa prediction based on evidence you can see nowIt’s going to be hard to get a job straightaway.
present continuousa fixed arrangement, usually with a time or a placeI’m taking a course at the University of Westminster.
present simplea timetable or schedule somebody else setsIt starts next week.
might / maya possibility, not a decisionI might find a job there too.
be likely toprobable, without committing to itThere are likely to be jobs you have never thought of.

Two of these are almost interchangeable and two are not. Will and going to often both work; the present continuous and the present simple do not swap, because one belongs to the speaker and the other to the timetable.

4 · One plan, five ways of saying it.
I think I’ll do a course next year.  →  an opinion, decided as I speak.

1 · Read the explanation.
The choice is about status, not about time

All the forms below refer to time after now, and none of them is a future tense. What you are choosing between is how settled the event is and where the decision came from.

Will is the neutral one. Use it for a prediction or an opinion about later, and for a decision you are taking as you speak: I think I will apply. It carries no evidence with it, which is why it is so often paired with probably, I expect, I think. Be going to does two jobs: it reports an intention you formed before this conversation (I am going to work in my parents’ shop), and it predicts from evidence you can point at now (unemployment is high, so it is going to be hard). The present continuous is for arrangements — the date is agreed, the place is booked, another person or an institution is involved. The present simple is for timetables: departures, terms, kick-off times, opening hours. It is the form you use when the schedule is not yours to change.

Degrees of certainty
  • certain: will definitely, is definitely going to, starts at nine
  • probable: will probably, is likely to, I expect, I doubt (for the negative)
  • possible: might, may, could, there is a chance that
  • Negatives behave differently: probably goes before won’t but after will — She will probably come / She probably won’t come.
2 · Study the examples.
PatternExample
will — predictionThere will be more jobs in health care within ten years.
will — prediction, hedgedIT skills will probably not be seen as a specialism.
will — instant decisionThat sounds useful. I’ll sign up tonight.
will — offer or promiseI’ll send you the details this evening.
going to — intentionI’m going to invest two hours a week in it.
going to — intention, negativeShe’s not going to accept the invitation.
going to — evidence nowLook at these figures. It’s going to be a hard year.
present continuous — arrangementI’m meeting the consultant on Thursday.
present continuous — arrangement, negativeWe’re not moving the meeting again.
present simple — timetableThe course starts next week and finishes in June.
present simple — timetable, questionWhat time does the session begin?
might / may — possibilityI might find a job there too.
be likely to — probabilityThere are likely to be jobs nobody has named yet.
be about to — the very near futureHurry — the programme is about to start.
after when, as soon as, afterWhen I finish the course, I’ll look for work abroad.
after ifIf it goes well, I’ll stay another year.
Two things to watch

1 — No will after when, as soon as, after, until or if. The time word already tells the reader it is the future, so the verb stays in the present: When I graduate, I will look for work — never when I will graduate. This is the single most common mistake at this level.

2 — Going to go is correct but clumsy. Native speakers usually say I’m going to Canada in September rather than I’m going to go to Canada. The present continuous does the job on its own with verbs of movement.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
There is no future tense; there is a choice

English has no future ending. It has forms you choose between, and the choice tells the listener how settled the thing is and where the evidence comes from.

will — a prediction or opinion about later, and the default with think, expect, probably, I’m sure: There will probably be more jobs in health care. It is also the form for a decision taken at the moment of speaking, and for offers and promises: That sounds useful. I’ll sign up tonight · I’ll send you the details this evening.

be going to — an intention decided before now (I’m going to work in my parents’ shop), or a prediction based on evidence you can see at this moment (Look at these figures. It’s going to be a hard year). The contrast with will is exactly this: will comes out of your head, going to out of a plan or the evidence in front of you.

Arrangements, timetables and hedging

present continuous — a fixed arrangement, normally with a time or a place attached: I’m taking a course at Westminster · I’m meeting the consultant on Thursday. Somebody else knows about it; a diary would show it. present simple — a timetable or schedule set by an institution: The course starts next week · The train leaves at six.

might / may mark a possibility rather than a decision (I might find a job there too), and be likely to is the neutral written version (Prices are likely to rise). In a subordinate clause of time, the future is not marked at all: When I finish the course, I will apply, never When I will finish.

Errors to watch: I will go to Almaty on Friday — it is booked → a fixed arrangement takes I’m going · Look at the sky, it will rain → evidence now: it’s going to rain · The train will leave at six according to the timetable → leaves · When I will arrive, I will call you → When I arrive…

Ten years from now

The programme wants a second episode, and this time the listeners are the guests.

The brief

Future Perfect is recording a short segment called Ten years from now. Each guest brings one prediction about their own field, one plan they have already made, and one thing they are considering but have not decided. The producers want the evidence behind the prediction, not the prediction on its own.

2 · Record the segment.
Useful language
  • Predicting: I expect… · It’s likely to… · There will probably be…
  • Evidence: You can see that already in… · Look at… — it’s going to…
  • Plans: I’m going to… · I’m …ing on the… · It starts in…
  • Hedging: I might… · It depends on whether… · I doubt I’ll…

1 · Read the model.
Model · a segment for the programme website

Ten years from now, almost nobody in my field will be paid for translating a menu or a contract. You can see it already: two of the four agencies in my city closed last year, and the work that is left is checking what a machine has produced. It is going to be a difficult decade for anybody who does only that.

So I am investing in the part a machine still cannot do. I am taking a course in conference interpreting in February — it starts on the eighth and runs for eleven months — and I have already turned down two invitations to work that would have made it impossible. When I finish, I intend to look for work with courts and hospitals rather than with agencies, because those rooms need a person in them.

I might also move to another country for a year, although that is likely to depend on the exchange rate rather than on me. What would prove me wrong is simple enough: if the machines learn to hear as well as they read, the whole plan needs a few large adjustments.
